common_name: Music Garlic (Extremely Popular Large-Clove Porcelain Hardneck)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Music is one of the most widely grown porcelain hardneck garlics in North America, prized for very large, easy-to-peel cloves.

directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Music is a Canadian-origin porcelain hardneck that has become one of the most popular garlic varieties in North America, producing large bulbs with just four to six exceptionally big, easy-to-peel cloves under bright white skin, and a rich, full, well-balanced flavor that holds up well raw or cooked. As a hardneck, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to redirect the plant's energy into bulb development; the scapes are edible and excellent in stir-fries or pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, then trim and store; Music has moderate storage life, typically five to seven months under good conditions.

common_name: Chesnok Red Garlic (Purple Stripe Hardneck, Prized for Roasting)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Chesnok Red is a purple stripe hardneck from the Republic of Georgia, especially prized for its mild, rich flavor when roasted or baked.

directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Chesnok Red, originally from the Republic of Georgia, is a purple stripe hardneck consistently rated by garlic growers as one of the best varieties for roasting and baking, since it stays mild and creamy rather than overpowering when cooked, while still carrying good pungency raw. Bulbs are medium-sized with striking purple-streaked skin over eight to ten easy-to-peel cloves. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to focus energy into the bulb; the scapes are excellent eaten fresh or cooked. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, and expect good but not exceptional storage life, typically four to six months.

common_name: Nootka Rose Garlic (Rocambole Hardneck with Rich Flavor)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Nootka Rose is a rocambole-type hardneck named for Nootka Sound in the Pacific Northwest, valued for rich flavor and attractive rose-tan bulb wrappers.

directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Nootka Rose is a rocambole-type hardneck garlic prized for rich, full-bodied flavor and attractive bulbs wrapped in rose-tan skin over large, easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single layer typical of rocamboles. Like other hardnecks, it sends up a dramatic double-curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to direct the plant's energy into bulb development; the scapes are excellent eaten fresh or cooked. Its rich flavor comes with the tradeoff of shorter storage life typical of rocamboles, generally four to five months, so plan to use it earlier in the storage season relative to porcelain or softneck types. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, and cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded location before trimming.

planting.note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Georgian Fire is a porcelain hardneck from the Republic of Georgia known for notably hot, spicy raw flavor.

directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Georgian Fire, originating from the Republic of Georgia, is a porcelain hardneck garlic valued for notably hot, spicy raw flavor that mellows into a rich, savory sweetness when roasted, along with large bulbs of four to six big, easy-to-peel cloves under smooth white skin typical of porcelain types. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to channel the plant's energy into bulb development; the scapes are edible and excellent in stir-fries or pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, then trim and store; porcelain types like Georgian Fire generally offer good storage life of six months or more under proper conditions.
